transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-20 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lina (Aurora CTO), Devon (ML infra), Samir (Principal Eng)

Auto-summary (note: auto-generated): quick deep-dive, lots of kernel-level questions, agreed to run more targeted benchs.

[00:00] Maya: all right thank you everyone for taking the time, um this is Maya from Redwood, i'll kick off, Ethan will drive the runtime profiling deep dive.
[00:12] Lina: thanks Maya, yeah super excited, we're evaluating both your hosted option and the dedicated cluster for some internal LLMs, and today we wanted to focus on GPU runtime behaviour.
[00:23] Ethan: great, i'll share my screen, but quick agenda: kernel selection heuristics, tensorrt-llm vs vllm microbenchmarks, cuda graphs warmup and capture overhead, kv-cache semantics, batching strategies, quantization caveats, and then we can map that to aurora's constraints. sound good?
[00:40] Devon: yep that works. our main goals: p95 < 150ms for 512-token requests for embeddings/rerank use cases, predictable cost, and data never leaving our VPC.
[00:52] Ethan: ok good, we'll try to hit those. starting with kernel selection: so our runtime profiles models at load time plus an online telemetry component. we look at op distribution, attention math patterns, and sequence length hist to pick kernels. sometimes the \"best\" kernel for long seqs hurts short seq p50 because of different memory access patterns.
[01:15] Samir: when you say kernel, are you selecting at op-level like flash-attention variant A vs B, or at cuBLAS vs custom fused ops?
[01:25] Ethan: both — we have a kernel selector that matches op type to candidate implementations: cuBLAS matmul, fused matmul+softmax, flash attention, Triton+cppfused, and also TensorRT-LLM plugins. selection uses microbenchmarks on startup and periodic sampling. note sometimes tensorrt picks a plugin that requires a specific tensor layout which then triggers a conversion cost for first few tokens.
[01:50] Lina: is that what causes the warmup spikes we saw in your shared dashboard? we saw p95 jumps on the first 100 tokens of a new prefix.
[02:02] Ethan: yeah exactly, that plus cuda graph capture. we rely on cuda graphs to amortize kernel launch overhead for autoregressive loops. the trick: graph capture needs a stable control flow and shapes; if batch size or seq length changes, capture invalidates and there's a re-capture penalty.
[02:20] Maya: and that's where kv cache prefix caching helps because if you see a lot of repeated prefixes you can serve from a cached kv snapshot and avoid recapture for subsequent queries.
[02:33] Devon: can you explain how you store kv snapshots and the memory overhead? we run many small sessions concurrently.
[02:40] Ethan: we snapshot the KV cache at token boundaries and store diffs in memory; for dedicated, we can pin that to GPU memory using a lightweight allocator. typical 7B-ish model kv per token is ~3-4MB; so for 1k tokens we're talking 3-4GB per session — so we prefer prefix-level caching (store only first N tokens) and LRU eviction. for high-concurrency workloads we recommend a hybrid: GPU pinned hot-cache for most frequent prefixes and DRAM for colder ones.
[03:20] Lina: ok that matches our concern. about tensorrt-llm vs vllm — we ran your sample microbench with a 2k seq and saw tensorrt had better throughput but worse latency tail. can you unpack that?
[03:34] Ethan: sure — TensorRT-LLM often wins when kernels are fused and quantization is used; it compiles highly optimized kernels that push throughput. but it also tends to favor larger batches and bigger launch granularity; so p99 suffers on small, latency-sensitive requests. vLLM (cpu/gpu runtime) is often more flexible with dynamic batching and smaller kernel footprints, resulting in better tail behavior for heterogeneous request sizes.
[03:58] Samir: are you seeing differences by model family? like Llama-like vs decoder-only vs mixture of experts?
[04:06] Ethan: yes — models with heavy rotary/ALiBi indexing or non-standard attention need specialized kernels; TensorRT sometimes can't fuse those efficiently and falls back to more generic kernels, which erases throughput wins. we maintain a catalog of model profiles and recommended runtime (tensorrt vs native) per model.
[04:28] Maya: a real-world example: we benchmarked a 13B open model at 512 context. vLLM-style runtime had lower p95 by ~30% at low concurrency, but TensorRT-LLM got 2.3x higher throughput at batch sizes >8 and when using int8 quantization.
[04:48] Devon: int8 — how do you validate quality after quantization? our finetuned models are sensitive to small numeric changes.
[04:55] Ethan: good question. we recommend an eval set of seeded prompts and compare perplexity and key task metrics; we also run A/B on a held-out prompt set and threshold on task-level drop. int8 often needs per-channel calibration and sometimes a small finetune with simulated quant noise. we also provide regression alerts in Redwood Optimize when quality shifts.
[05:25] Lina: the CUDA graphs comment earlier — how long is the re-capture penalty? we saw a 200-400ms spike.
[05:32] Ethan: re-capture depends on graph size and kernel count; small graphs re-capture in ~30-80ms; large autoregressive graphs with many ops and custom kernels can be 200-500ms. plus you might see a cold cache Effects where memory is paged in. we mitigate by pre-capturing common shapes during deployment and keeping a small pool of already-captured variants.
[06:05] Devon: can you show traces?
[06:08] Ethan: yes opening the benchmark spreadsheet I shared earlier — um, apologies if labels are messy, auto-exports sometimes flip names — on the first sheet you can see tensorrt vs vllm: p50/p95/p99 for 512/1k sequences at batch sizes 1,4,8.
[06:25] [screen share noise]
[06:40] Ethan: the trace here shows a capture event at t=0 for a 512 token run, p95 spike around 0.45s, then steady-state p50 ~80ms. note the spikes line up with GPU kernel fallbacks.
[06:55] Samir: do you instrument kernel choice per invocation so we can correlate with our telemetry?
[07:01] Ethan: yes we emit per-request kernel fingerprint + process id, and you can join that with your logs. for private deployments we can forward the traces to your internal observability — we support OTLP export in the private control plane.
[07:18] Lina: VPC/on-prem — what changes for kernel selection or cuda graph behavior in air-gapped setups?
[07:26] Ethan: functionally nothing changes, but the initial startup microbench that runs in hosted mode to pick kernels needs to be run in your environment, so sometimes we include a profiling step during install. also for HSM/KMS integration we don't ship keys — we integrate with your KMS endpoints. upgrade cycles are a bit more manual in private.
[07:45] Devon: we have an HSM and strict egress rules; can the runtime call home only for optional telemetry?
[07:52] Maya: yes, telemetry can be disabled; we provide an offline telemetry bundle you can extract and share with Redwood SEs. required heartbeats are optional in private deployments.
[08:05] Ethan: back to batching — we support dynamic batching with target latency windows. basically you define a max latency SLO and a queue policy, and the runtime will accumulate tokens up to a shape budget. dynamic batching avoids high tail when arrival patterns are bursty, but it can increase token duplication if you don't use prefix caching.
[08:32] Lina: any guidance on shape bucketing? our traffic is mix of 64 to 1024 token requests, modal at ~256.
[08:40] Ethan: recommend two buckets: short (<=256) and long (257-1024). keep short bucket aggressive with low batch thresholds, long bucket larger. also configure an adaptive policy that shifts thresholds during peak windows.
[08:55] Samir: what about memory pressure with pinned kv caches plus batching? we saw OOMs in one test.
[09:02] Ethan: OOMs often come from naive kv pinning across many sessions. Our advice: cap pinned kv per-GPU, evict least-used prefixes, and use a memory-aware scheduler that will move cooler prefixes to host DRAM or persist to disk. dedicated clusters can be configured with larger GPU resident pools if you need consistent low-latency.
[09:25] Devon: can you quantify the throughput/latency delta for quantization at our 13B model?
[09:30] Ethan: approximate numbers from our tests: fp16 baseline p50 ~120ms for 512 tokens; int8 tuned p50 ~70ms and throughput +2.2x, but p95 can increase if calibration is off. 4-bit quant can reduce memory by ~2x but often needs more careful per-channel scaling; quality drop depends on your prompts.
[09:52] Lina: ok useful. about evaluation — can you run a small pilot with our finetuned 13B and our 30 prompt eval set?
[09:58] Maya: yes that's the pilot we proposed — we'll provision a dedicated node and run the bench with both runtimes and quant profiles. we'll need your sample model and eval prompts.
[10:08] Samir: sharing model might be sensitive — we can share a masked/stripped checkpoint and the prompt set.
[10:14] Ethan: that works — for kernel-level debugging we may ask for a small representative binary or a subset of weights, but we can often reproduce behaviour with the model architecture + calibration files.
[10:26] Lina: you mentioned tensorrt plugin conversions — does Redwood provide conversion tooling or do we have to run tensorrt-llm ourselves?
[10:33] Ethan: we provide conversion tooling as an optional pipeline. for private deployments we can run conversions in your environment or provide a conversion container. conversions sometimes require CUDA Toolkit specific versions — we'll share a compatibility matrix.
[10:48] Devon: compatibility with multi-GPU sharding? our 8xA100 cluster uses tensor-parallel sharding and we want to avoid cross-node kv traffic.
[10:57] Ethan: our runtime supports model parallelism strategies: tensor parallel intra-node, and we prefer sharded KV layouts that avoid cross-node fetches during generation; cross-node traffic happens on attention recompute or when KV caching is remote. Dedicated can be provisioned with NVLink topology to minimize cross-GPU traffic.
[11:20] Lina: any gotchas with cudagraphs and model-parallel runs?
[11:24] Ethan: yes — cudagraphs assume a fixed sequence of CUDA launches; when using model parallel with cross-GPU syncs, graph capture can be more fragile. we recommend capturing per-device graphs and stitching them with a small runtime shim. that's a bit more advanced but we've done it for large-infra customers.
[11:45] Samir: what's the typical cadence for kernel selector updates? do you push new heuristics frequently?
[11:50] Ethan: we push periodic selector updates via the control plane for hosted and dedicated flows, roughly weekly to monthly depending on upstream kernel releases (cuBLAS, cuDNN, TRT). for private, we ship selector updates that you can opt into; they are non-breaking but we recommend running them in staging first.
[12:07] Maya: ok shifting to the pilot scope, proposed tests: 1) cold-start capture + warm steady-state 512/1k runs, 2) concurrency matrix for batch sizes 1/4/8, 3) quantization sweeps (fp16/int8/4bit) with eval set, 4) KV prefix stress test.
[12:25] Lina: yes please include CUDA graph capture events and per-kernel timings; we want the raw traces.
[12:31] Ethan: we'll include Nsight and CUPTI level traces; note the raw files can be large, we'll provide a summarized view too.
[12:40] Devon: about legal/compliance — we need to be sure logs don't leak PII and that audit logs are available.
[12:46] Maya: Redwood Private supports audit logs and integrates with your SIEM; we'll include the SOC2 scope docs in the security packet.
[12:54] Lina: timeline? we'd like pilot started before new-year.
[12:58] Maya: we'll aim to provision the dedicated nodes in the week of Dec 27th, run profiling the following week. depends on Aurora's availability to share the model and confirm the window.
[13:10] Ethan: ok i'll run the initial microbench this week to sanity-check kernel choices, then do the full captures during the pilot.
[13:18] Samir: one more question — how do you handle graceful degradation if a plugin fails at runtime?
[13:24] Ethan: we have an automatic fallback policy: if a kernel/ plugin fails or gets a fatal on launch, the runtime falls back to compatible generic kernels and optionally sinks the request to a lower-cost route (e.g., hosted in another region) if configured. fallback is logged and can trigger auto-rollbacks if regressions are detected.
[13:43] Lina: perfect. thanks everyone, this was helpful.
